summaries.example: Imagine that Maya hears a bell but cannot see where it came from. She thinks the bell might be in the hall or the playground. If it is in both places that she still considers possible, she does not know where it is. If every possibility she can think of has the bell in the hall, then the model says Maya knows the bell is in the hall. The model can also represent whether Maya knows that she knows this.
summaries.summary: Epistemic logic is a part of logic about knowledge, belief, and information. It uses symbols such as K for “knows” and B for “believes.” A common method imagines several possible worlds, or ways things could be. An agent’s information connects the worlds that the agent cannot tell apart. A claim counts as known when it is true in all of those connected worlds. This lets us study simple knowledge, knowledge about someone else’s knowledge, and knowledge shared by groups. The method also raises questions. For example, should knowledge always be true? Should a person who knows one fact automatically know every fact that logically follows from it? The entry also discusses knowledge of what, who, why, and how, as well as the problem that formal systems may give agents unrealistically perfect reasoning abilities.
key_ideas: Epistemic logic studies knowledge and belief with carefully designed symbols and rules.
An agent knows a claim when that claim is true in every situation the agent still considers possible.
The logic can describe higher-order knowledge, such as knowing that someone knows something.
Different rules about the links between possible worlds produce different ideas about knowledge.
The subject is used in philosophy, computer science, artificial intelligence, and economics.
summaries.why_it_matters: People and groups often need to decide what is known, what is only believed, and what remains uncertain. Epistemic logic gives researchers a precise way to describe these situations. It can help model communication, teamwork, computer systems, artificial intelligence, and games in which people reason about one another. It also reminds us that a neat mathematical model may leave out real limits on attention, memory, or reasoning.

important_terms.definition: The study of using logic to describe knowledge, belief, and uncertainty.
A statement that can be true or false, such as “the bell is in the hall.”
A way things might be, especially a way that fits what an agent knows.
A symbol used to say that an agent knows something. Kₐφ means “agent a knows that φ.”
A map of possible worlds and the links between worlds that an agent cannot tell apart.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone believe something that is not true? How is that different from knowing it?
If Maya knows a fact, must she also know that she knows it?
What information would help an agent rule out a possible world?
Is it fair to say a person knows every logical result of what they know?

summaries.example: Suppose two students, A and B, receive different clues about whether a key is in Box 1 or Box 2. A can distinguish the boxes, but B cannot. A formula such as K_A(p) can represent that A knows proposition p, while K_B(p) may be false. We can also write K_B K_A(p) to ask whether B knows that A knows p. If a teacher publicly announces a true clue, the set of worlds compatible with the students’ information changes. Dynamic epistemic logic studies this update. The example shows why simply saying “everyone knows p” is weaker than saying “it is common knowledge that p”: common knowledge includes indefinitely many levels of knowing that others know.
summaries.summary: Epistemic logic applies formal logic to knowledge, belief, and related informational attitudes. Its standard modal language includes Kₐφ for “agent a knows that φ” and Bₐφ for “agent a believes that φ.” In Kripke-style semantics, a model contains possible worlds, truth assignments for basic propositions, and accessibility relations representing which worlds an agent cannot exclude. Knowledge is then evaluated universally across the accessible worlds. This semantics connects formal principles with structural properties: reflexivity supports the truth principle, symmetry supports a form of negative-looking possibility reasoning, and transitivity supports positive introspection. With several agents, the language can express nested knowledge, distributed knowledge, everybody-knows claims, and common knowledge. Public-announcement operators model information change. The entry also surveys formal treatments of know-wh expressions and examines logical omniscience, the worry that standard systems attribute perfect logical closure to agents whose reasoning is actually limited. Different logics and models respond to these issues in different ways; the entry does not treat one solution as settled.
key_ideas: Epistemic logic represents knowing-that and believing-that with modal operators, and can nest these operators to express higher-order attitudes.
In possible-world semantics, Kₐφ is true when φ holds in every world compatible with agent a’s information.
The properties of an accessibility relation correspond to principles such as truthfulness, positive introspection, and negative introspection.
Knowledge and belief need not receive the same treatment: knowledge is commonly modeled as veridical, while belief is often modeled as consistent without requiring truth.
Multi-agent systems distinguish individual knowledge, distributed knowledge, everybody-knows claims, and common knowledge.
The framework extends to public announcements and to forms of knowing-what, knowing-who, knowing-why, and knowing-how, but these extensions introduce further technical choices.
summaries.why_it_matters: Epistemic logic provides a bridge between philosophical questions about knowledge and formal models used in computer science, artificial intelligence, economics, and the study of group interaction. It makes assumptions visible. For example, choosing an equivalence relation commits a model to particular principles about what agents can know about their own information. Choosing weaker relations permits different theories. The framework is therefore useful not only for proving consequences but also for testing whether a proposed account of knowledge, belief, or communication is plausible.

important_terms.definition: A formal approach to knowledge and belief, usually using modal logic.
A statement treated as a basic unit in a formal language, with a truth value in a model.
A modal symbol for knowledge; Kₐφ means that agent a knows φ.
A formal structure with possible worlds, a relation between worlds, and a valuation assigning truth to propositions.
A relation in which every world is linked to itself, linked worlds link back to one another, and links chain together.
Knowledge that would result from pooling the information of the members of a group.
A group’s fact being known by everyone, everyone knowing that everyone knows it, and so on without end.
The concern that formal agents know all logical consequences of what they know, despite limited human reasoning.

questions_to_think_about: Should the principle “if an agent knows φ, then the agent knows that it knows φ” hold for ordinary human knowledge?
Why might common knowledge require more than a finite list of “everyone knows” statements?
Which is more plausible for belief: truthfulness, consistency, or neither?
Does a formal model explain actual knowledge, or only an idealized form of it?
When should two notions such as knowledge and belief be kept distinct rather than combined?

summaries.example: A class is trying to find a hidden flag. Sam hears that the flag is either near the library or the gym, but cannot tell which. Lee sees a clue showing it is near the library. Sam may not know where the flag is, while Lee does. Sam might also wonder whether Lee knows. In a model, each possible location is a possible world, and links connect worlds that an agent cannot distinguish. If the teacher truthfully announces, “The flag is not near the gym,” some worlds disappear from consideration. The updated model represents what the students know after the announcement.
summaries.summary: Epistemic logic is the formal study of knowledge, belief, and information. It commonly uses modal logic: Kₐφ says that agent a knows φ, while Bₐφ says that a believes φ. The main semantic idea is to represent information with possible worlds. From a given world, an agent has access to the worlds that fit what the agent cannot distinguish. Kₐφ is true when φ holds in all those worlds. This approach supports nested claims, such as an agent knowing that another agent knows something. It also links philosophical principles to features of the model. Reflexivity is connected with the idea that known claims are true; transitivity is connected with positive introspection; and symmetry is connected with another strong principle about an agent’s awareness of its own uncertainty. For groups, the theory distinguishes information held by each individual, information that would emerge by combining their clues, and common knowledge. The entry further discusses dynamic updates, know-what and know-how, and logical omniscience—the challenge that formal agents may reason far better than real people.
key_ideas: Epistemic logic uses modal operators to represent what particular agents know or believe.
Possible-world models explain uncertainty by tracking which situations an agent has not ruled out.
Formal principles about knowledge correspond to properties of the accessibility relation, such as reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity.
Knowledge is usually treated as factive or veridical: if someone knows a claim, the claim is true. Belief is often treated differently.
Group models can represent nested knowledge, pooled information, everybody-knows information, and common knowledge.
The field also studies information changes, richer forms of knowing, and ways to avoid modeling people as perfect reasoners.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many situations depend on what people know about one another: cooperation, communication, games, social rules, and computer networks are examples discussed by the field. Epistemic logic helps separate assumptions that are easy to blur in ordinary speech. A model can show whether a claim is true, whether an agent can rule out alternatives, and whether everyone knows that everyone knows it. At the same time, the problem of logical omniscience shows why a successful formal model may need to idealize or add extra machinery to represent limited human awareness and reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A branch of logic that studies knowledge, belief, and information using formal systems.
A statement that can be evaluated as true or false in a situation.
A possible way the relevant facts could be arranged; it need not be the actual situation.
A connection between worlds that an agent’s information does not distinguish.
A formal model containing worlds, relations between them, and truth assignments for basic statements.
Knowledge about another agent’s knowledge or belief, often represented by nested operators such as KₐKᵦp.
A group condition in which a fact is known at every level: everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so forth.
The problem that ideal formal agents may know every logical consequence, unlike people with limited time and reasoning abilities.

questions_to_think_about: If two people have different evidence, can one know something the other does not?
Why is “everyone knows the rule” different from “the rule is common knowledge”?
Should knowing a fact guarantee knowing that you know it?
What would a model need to represent a person who has not noticed a relevant possibility?
How could a system avoid giving a limited human agent every logical consequence of its information?
